captions.threads:
1/3
There is a strange thing that happens when you open your own work after a week away. The files are yours, the name on the folder is yours, and yet the whole thing reads like a note left by someone who understood the problem better than you do right now. Distance does not just cool the work. It changes the person holding it.

2/3
Maybe that is the paradox. The stranger in the folder is still you, just a you that was paying attention. The distraction did not erase your ability to make things. It only pulled you into a different rhythm, one built for novelty instead of continuity, and continuity is what the project needed from you.

3/3
So the question I keep circling is whether the discomfort of re-entry is a signal to resist or a kind of translation you have to do before the work can speak again. If the stranger is you, what would it mean to introduce yourself properly before asking anything of the work?

captions.threads:
1/4
The fastest song I ever made sounded finished, and I hated it immediately. Eleven minutes, perfect mix, zero me in it. Faster isn't the same as better, and I keep bumping into that.

2/4
So I don't want to throw the tools out. They're useful. They hand me ideas I'd never have reached on my own. But the output arrives looking complete, and that's exactly the trap. Polish can pass for meaning until you listen closely.

3/4
Still not sure where the line sits. Some days a rough generated chord loop turns into the spine of something real. Other days I'm just sanding down someone else's guess. I'm learning to notice which one I'm doing before I've lost an afternoon to it.
